paragraphs: The Author said: When the discourse on the purification of action for God alone has come before us, and self-conceit with respect to purified action is the swiftest among the misfortunes that attach to those who have purification, and its corrupting of the works is very great — I saw that what is most emphasized in following upon that is what negates self-conceit from the human, namely humility.

Likewise, since it has also been validly established for us that humility is the root of slavehood — that by it the slave is severed from the attributes of lordship, and acknowledges to God (exalted be He) that He alone has them and is unique in them to the exclusion of created beings, as the Friend (peace be upon him) said: "Yours, O Lord, are the greatness and the might and the splendor and the victory and the majesty; for everything in the heavens and in the earth is Yours; Yours, O Lord, is the kingdom, and the One who is exalted as head over all" (1 Chronicles 29:11); and he said: "For who in the cloud can be ranked with the Lord? Who can be likened to the Lord among the divine beings?" (Psalms 89:7) — and since it is also among its concerns that it negates from the human pride, vainglory, conceit, haughtiness, self-glorification, exaltation, ostentation, magnification, overstepping toward the weak, longing for what is above him, and what resembles these, of the branches of self-conceit:
It is fitting now that I explicate the matter of humility in ten concepts:

1. **The first**: what humility is. 2. **The second**: into how many divisions it is divided. 3. **The third**: from what humility arises. 4. **The fourth**: in what its use is incumbent. 5. **The fifth**: how the aspects of acquiring it are. 6. **The sixth**: on the description of the conduct that the humble man must follow. 7. **The seventh**: when humility from the humble is genuine, and when it is not made valid. 8. **The eighth**: that we make plain whether humility is consequent upon the excellences or the excellences are consequent upon it. 9. **The ninth**: whether self-conceit and humility may be gathered in the heart of the human, or not. 10. **The tenth**: the explication of the benefit of humility in the matters of this world and the next.
As for what humility is —

I say that it is the abasement of the soul, its self-lowering, and the smallness of its measure in its own sight. It is a trait among the traits of the soul. When it is firmly fixed in the soul, its marks appear upon the limbs: among them, gentleness of speech, the lowering of the voice, forbearance at the time of anger, slightness of self-vindication after the capacity for it. As was said of one of the princes — that he said to one who deserved punishment from him, after the lash was readied: "By God! Were it not for the severity of my anger against you, I would have inflicted upon you the harshest punishment." And he pardoned him. It was said of him that he used to say: "I know no offense weightier than my forbearance."
As for the explication of the divisions of humility —
Humility is divided into three divisions.

**The first** is general to the human and to many of the kinds of the non-rational animal. It is the dullness of the soul and its bearing-with-patience the harm it could ward off, out of its ignorance of the aspects of warding it off. This is found among the ignorant of people and the populace, on account of the slightness of their acquaintance, and the weakness of their discrimination of themselves and their measures. This is called "humility" only by way of convention; in true reality it is the weakness of the soul and its blindness from the ignorance overwhelming it concerning what would set it right — as the Friend said: "For You have hidden their heart from understanding; therefore You shall not exalt them" (Job 17:4).

True humility is what occurs after the elevation of aspiration, and the lofty disdain for sharing with the beasts in the blameworthy traits, and the towering above resemblance to the traits of the lowly populace — by surpassing knowledge, dignity of soul, and the true reality of acquaintance with the excellences and the vices. When upon this there follow the abasement of the soul and its self-lowering, this is praiseworthy. What is other than this does not enter into the praiseworthy traits and the excellences of the soul; rather it enters into their blameworthy ones. For its possessor's reckoning in this is the reckoning of the beasts.

**The second division** is humility before people. It is either on account of their dominion over him — like the captive in the hand of his enemy and the slave in the presence of his master — or on account of his poverty toward them and the emphatic need of his to what is in their hand: like the hireling toward his employer, the poor man toward the help of the wealthy man, the disciple toward his teacher. Or it may be on account of an obligatory right and a binding debt upon him that the human is unable to discharge — and so humility and abasement to the holder of the right are binding upon him, as the Wise One said: "The borrower is slave to the lender" (Proverbs 22:7). Or it may be on account of his knowledge of his falling-short in the kinds of cultivation of this world and the next, and his ignorance of the road of guidance — so that, when his hand obtains a prophet of his time, or a saint who guides, or one who calls to the path of right-direction, he humbles himself before him and lowers himself in his presence — as our early ones (peace be upon them) said: "The service of [the wise] is greater than the learning from them, as it is said: 'Here is Elisha son of Shaphat, who poured water upon the hands of Elijah' (2 Kings 3:11) — it does not say 'who learned' but 'who poured'; this teaches that the service of them is greater than the learning from them" (b. Berakhot 7b); and He said: "And his servant Joshua son of Nun, a youth, did not depart from the tent" (Exodus 33:11); and the Wise One said of the totality of the populace: "The slave of the fool is to the wise of heart" (Proverbs 11:29).

This division of the divisions of humility, even if it is necessary in nature, is not among the lofty excellences absolutely. For it is not common to all rational beings, nor is it incumbent upon them at every time and in every place. The captive, when he is released from his captivity; the slave, when his neck is freed; the debtor, when he discharges his debt; the disciple, when he is absent from his teacher; the poor man, when he becomes free of need of what is in the hands of people — humility, abasement, and lowering before them are not binding upon him.

**The third division** is humility before God (exalted be He). It is comprehensive in its obligation upon all the rational beings, and incumbent upon them at every time and in every place. To it our intent is directed in this gate. The humble man is the one named in the Book of God: ʿanav, *nivzeh be-ʿeinav*, *tzanuaʿ*, *dakhʾ*, *shefal ruaḥ*, *ruaḥ nishbarah*, *nidkeh*, *rakh leivav*, *nekhe-ruaḥ*, *lev nishbar*, *nefesh shaḥah*.

What we have said in our discourse on humility absolutely refers to this third division alone — which is the highest degree of humility. He for whom it is validly attained, the path of nearing to God and drawing-close to Him is not far from him; God receives his work from him and is satisfied with him, as He said: "The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a heart broken and crushed, O God, You shall not despise" (Psalms 51:19).
As for the causes from which abasement, lowering, and humility arise in the human after his towering — they are ten.

**The first**: when his strength weakens from his natural movement on account of sicknesses, bad mixture-of-humors, or weakness of his composition; he humbles himself and is lowered before the Creator (exalted be He) and before people, as He said: "And He brought down their heart with toil; they stumbled, and there was no helper" (Psalms 107:12).

**The second**: when the misfortune of poverty and the need of people befalls him after his self-sufficiency from them; he humbles himself before them, and his aspiration is broken from self-conceit at his state, as He said: "And it shall be that everyone left in your house shall come to bow down to him for a piece of silver and a loaf of bread, and shall say: 'Add me, I pray, to one of the priestly classes, that I may eat a piece of bread'" (1 Samuel 2:36).

**The third**: when blessing has been poured out upon another and his bounty has been made manifest over him; he humbles himself before him, as He said: "Many entreat the favor of the noble" (Proverbs 19:6).

**The fourth**: when an obligation toward another is incumbent upon him and he is weak in discharging it; he humbles himself before him, as He said: "If you have nothing to pay, why should he take your bed from under you?" (Proverbs 22:27).

**The fifth**: when he is in the captivity of his enemy; he humbles himself before him and his soul is lowered, as He said: "They afflicted his foot with shackles, his soul came into iron" (Psalms 105:18); and He said: "And if they are bound in fetters, taken in cords of affliction" (Job 36:8).

**The sixth**: when he is an enslaved slave with no power to free his neck from the hand of his owner; he humbles himself before him, as He said: "Behold, as the eyes of slaves to the hand of their masters, as the eyes of a maidservant to the hand of her mistress, so are our eyes upon the Lord our God, until He has mercy upon us" (Psalms 123:2).

**The seventh**: when severities and saddening calamities descend upon the human; his soul is broken and he is humbled, as He said: "Or if their uncircumcised heart is then humbled" (Leviticus 26:41).

**The eighth**: when he reckons with himself for his disobedience to God in the face of His blessing, and his transgressing through the blessing in place of thanks for it; he humbles himself, is abashed, and is shamed before God (exalted be He), as He said: "O my God, I am ashamed and put to the blush, to lift up, my God, my face to You; for our iniquities have multiplied above the head, and our guilt is great unto the heavens" (Ezra 9:6).

**The ninth**: when God's reproach and rebuke for opposition to His obedience comes upon him; he humbles himself and is alarmed, as He said of Ahab: "Have you seen how Ahab has humbled himself before Me?" (1 Kings 21:29).

**The tenth**: when he senses the nearness of death and the descent of fate upon him, and reflects on the terror of death and the standing of the reckoning; he humbles himself and is lowered, his soul becomes contemptible to him, and he regrets the passing of his life and the ending of his term without provision of good work he might bring forward in his presence at his departure — as He said: "The sinners in Zion are in dread; trembling has seized the impious: 'Who among us shall dwell with a devouring fire? Who among us shall dwell with everlasting burnings?'" (Isaiah 33:14).
As for that in which the use of humility and abasement is incumbent upon the human —
I say: humility is binding upon the human in its use in seven concepts.

**The first**: in his dealings with the people of his time and his treatment of the children of his species — according to what we shall set forth in what we resume. Of this Scripture says: "He is despised in his own eyes, contemptible — but he honors those who fear the Lord; he has sworn to do harm and does not change" (Psalms 15:4).

**The second**: when he meets the people of knowledge of God and of His Law, and the people of righteousness and nearness-to-God, as He said: "Let the righteous strike me in kindness and rebuke me" (Psalms 141:5); and He said: "The wicked bow down before the good, and the wicked at the gates of the righteous" (Proverbs 14:19).

**The third**: when he is praised for his excellences. It is incumbent upon him to humble himself, and to bring to mind what has gone before for him with God of sins and offenses that are in God's knowledge — and His covering of them, and the length of His granting him reprieve until he repents of them; let the people's mistake about him not delight him, but rather let him grieve at the soundness of God's knowledge of his ill dealings with Him and his heedlessness of discharging the right of His blessing upon him; let him humble himself within himself, as He said: "For my iniquity I shall declare; I shall be anxious for my sin" (Psalms 38:19).

**The fourth**: when he is reproached for his bad work. Let him humble himself before God and thank Him who has uncovered upon him a little of much, by way of disciplining him and reproving him that he may repent — as He said: "And He uncovers their ear to discipline, and says that they should turn from iniquity" (Job 36:10).

**The fifth**: when God grants him blessing in this world of various kinds of blessings. Let him humble himself before God for the heaviness of his back with the right of thanks for them; let him be lowered before Him out of fear that it should be a vengeance upon him.
For the abundance of wealth in this world is for one of three things. Either a blessing from God upon the possessor of wealth, or a trial and testing for him, or a vengeance and temptation upon him.

The mark of *blessing*: the possessor of it is preoccupied with the upholding of the rights of God by it, away from being preoccupied *with it*. It becomes a cause of his increasing in work for God; he does not crowd around it nor lean upon it, but disburses it in what God (exalted be He) has made obligatory upon him — like Job's description of his way of life with his wealth and his disbursing of it in the right of God; then he said, of the slightness of his reliance upon it: "If I have made gold my confidence, and to the fine gold said, 'You are my trust'…" (Job 31:24).

The mark of *trial and testing*: the possessor of wealth has been preoccupied with care for keeping the wealth, with increasing it, and with guarding it from misfortunes — away from upholding thanks to God for it. Its possessor is being tested by it; he gets nothing from it but the long preoccupation, the upkeep, and the reckoning concerning it. Of him the Wise One said: "For all his days are pains, and his task is grief; even at night his heart does not rest" (Ecclesiastes 2:23).

The mark of *vengeance*: the possessor of wealth has been preoccupied by enjoyment of it and pleasure in it from discharging the rights of God and the rights of people that are upon him from it; he has forgotten the One who blesses, and does not perceive what is binding upon him from it of obedience and slavehood — as Scripture said: "And behold, joy and gladness, slaying oxen and slaughtering sheep, eating flesh and drinking wine: 'Eat and drink, for tomorrow we die'" (Isaiah 22:13); and He said: "And there shall be lyre and lute, drum and pipe, and wine at their banquets — but the work of the Lord they regard not, and the deed of His hands they do not see" (Isaiah 5:12). That is vengeance in the form of blessing.

The intelligent man, when blessing comes upon him and the world turns toward him with what he loves of its matters — let him humble himself, out of fear that it be a vengeance from God upon him, as the Wise One said: "Wealth kept by its owner to his harm" (Ecclesiastes 5:12).

**The sixth**: when he reads the Book of God and the books of the prophets, with their promise and their threat, and recognizes from himself a falling-short in the rights of God and of the people of his time — humility and self-lowering before God (exalted be He) are incumbent upon him out of fear of His punishment, as He said of Josiah (peace be upon him): "And it was, when the king heard the words of the Book of the Law, that he tore his garments" (2 Kings 22:11); and God said to him: "Because your heart was tender, and you humbled yourself before the Lord when you heard what I had spoken about this place and against its dwellers, that they should become a desolation and a curse, and you tore your garments and wept before Me — even I have heard, says the Lord" (2 Kings 22:19).

**The seventh**: when he undertakes the doing of any of the works of obedience to God — like prayer, charity, a Law-precept, a supererogatory act, or an admonition — let him not undertake that with anything in his heart of conceit or pride; rather let him humble himself and abase himself before God in his outer and his inner. Let his measure not be great in his own sight in the face of the magnitude of what is binding upon him toward God in the like of that work, as He said: "With what shall I come before the Lord? With what shall I bow myself before the high God? Will the Lord be pleased with thousands of rams, with ten thousand rivers of oil?" — He said: "He has told you, O man, what is good, and what does the Lord seek of you but to do justice and to love kindness and to walk humbly with your God?" (Micah 6:6, 8).
As for the aspects of acquiring the trait of humility and the road of making it easy upon the human —
That comes about by attending in thought and turning the inward attention to seven things.

**The first**: the root of his coming-to-be and the beginning of his origin from semen and blood, after their decay and the foulness of their odor; then his nourishment by the blood of menses for the duration of his being in the belly of his mother; then his coming forth in a state of weakness, of frailty of body and limb; then his ascent from this rank to the next, until he reaches his maturity; then his taking-up into old age, until the conclusion of his term. One of the sages said in this concept: "I marvel at one who passes urine through the channel of urination twice — how he is proud and tilts his nose." Reflection on this and on its like of the human's affair makes humility binding upon him; for this reason the Friend (peace be upon him) said: "Lord, what is the human, that You take note of him; the son of man, that You give thought to him?" (Psalms 144:3); and he said: "Man born of woman is short of days and full of agitation" (Job 14:1); and he said: "But I am a worm and not a man" (Psalms 22:7); and he said: "How much less, then, man — a worm — and the son of man — a maggot" (Job 25:6).

**The second**: when he reflects on the magnitude of what has met him in this world of the kinds of trial — by hunger, thirst, heat, cold, sicknesses, calamities, and anxieties from which he has no rest except by death — and when the discerning man has gathered all of this and become sharp to his weakness and the slightness of his perception of what would ward this off from his soul, he discriminates from the picture of his standing that he is like a captive in this abode (rather, he is so in true reality); and he humbles himself with the humility of the imprisoned captive who has no contrivance and no power for the freeing of his soul without the satisfaction of his master with him, as He said: "Let the groan of the captive come before You" (Psalms 79:11); and: "Bring my soul out of prison, that I may give thanks to Your name" (Psalms 142:8).

**The third**: when he reflects on the conclusion of his term and the swiftness of the descent of death upon him; the cutting-off of his hope and his expectation at that; his abandonment of his affairs and his despair of provisioning himself with anything from them or benefiting by them; the picture of his standing in the grave — the light of his face having gone, his color blackened, the worms and the rot and the pus having fallen upon him, the traces of the beauties of his body departed, the foulness of his odor intensified as if he had never been bathed nor cleaned nor scented with the like of perfumes. When the like of this and its likes has occurred to the human's mind, he humbles himself within himself; he is lowered; he is not conceited, does not tower, no vanity or pride enters him — as Scripture said: "Cease from man, in whose nostril is breath; for in what is he to be reckoned?" (Isaiah 2:22); and He said: "Surely the children of man are vapor; the children of men are a lie" (Psalms 62:10).

**The fourth**: when he brings to mind what is binding upon him of obedience to God on account of His abundant bounty toward him and His lavish beneficence to him; his turning aside from the rational and the heard-revealed laws and his falling-short in them; the cutting-off of his case and the narrowing of excuses upon him on the day of the reckoning; and his regret in the standing of the requital — he humbles himself, is lowered, his soul is broken, as He said: "For behold, the day comes, burning like an oven, and all the proud and all the doers of wickedness shall be stubble; and the day that comes shall set them ablaze, says the Lord of hosts, that shall leave them neither root nor branch" (Malachi 3:19); and He said: "Who can endure the day of His coming, and who shall stand at His appearing? For He is like a refiner's fire and like fullers' soap" (Malachi 3:2).

**The fifth**: when he reflects on the majesty of the Creator (exalted be He) and the piercing of His power, the One who is overseeing his outer and his inner — and there falls into his soul this momentous matter, as the early ones mentioned of many of the excellent ones of preceding ages, of the awe and the majesty; so too their saying: "He set his eyes upon him and he became a heap of bones" (b. Berakhot 58a); and they said of Jonathan ben Uzziel: "When he expounded Torah, every bird that flew over him was burned up" (b. Sukkah 28a). There is no doubt that the rank of the prophets is above their rank; and you find the prophets — their strengths poured out, falling prostrate at their meeting with the angels — as in Daniel and Ezekiel and Joshua, and many like them. You find in the Truthful Book that the angels themselves fall prostrate to God (exalted be He), as He said: "And the host of heaven bows down to You" (Nehemiah 9:6); and He said: "Behold, in His servants He places no trust, and His angels He charges with imperfection" (Job 4:18); and He said: "And in His sanctuary all of it says: Glory!" (Psalms 29:9); and He said: "And one cried to another…" (Isaiah 6:3).

There is in what is manifest to our intellects from the side of His made things — like the sun and the moon and the stars and the celestial sphere and the earth and what is upon it of inanimate, plant, and animal — sufficiency for one who has understood and reasoned, as He said: "How great are Your works, O Lord — very deep are Your thoughts; the brutish man does not know, and the fool does not understand this" (Psalms 92:6–7); and He said: "All the nations are as nothing before Him" (Isaiah 40:17); and He said in the Targum: "All the inhabitants of the earth are as nothing reckoned." When the discerning, sharp man reflects on his proportion to the rational beings, and the proportion of the rational beings to the globe of the earth, and the proportion of the earth to the sphere of the moon, and the sphere of the moon to the highest sphere; and the totality of that, in the face of the power of the Creator (exalted be He), has no proportion and no measure — he sees the measure of the human, in the face of the power of the Creator, as nothing. He humbles himself within himself and is lowered before his Creator, as He said: "What is the human, that You remember him; the son of man, that You take note of him?" (Psalms 8:5).

**The sixth**: when he reads the Book of God and sees the severity of God's punishment and His threat to the people of magnification and self-glorification, and the intensity of His care for the humble and the lowered — he humbles himself and is lowered, as He said concerning the people of self-elevation and towering: "The lofty looks of man shall be brought low, and the haughtiness of men shall be bowed down; and the Lord alone shall be exalted on that day; for the day of the Lord of hosts shall be upon every proud and lofty one, and upon every lifted up and brought low" (Isaiah 2:11–12); and He said concerning the two ranks: "The Lord lifts up the humble, He brings down the wicked to the earth" (Psalms 147:6); and He said: "For the Lord is exalted, and sees the lowly" (Psalms 138:6); and He said concerning the humble: "And the humble shall inherit the land and shall delight in the abundance of peace" (Psalms 37:11); and: "Because the Lord has anointed Me to bring good news to the humble; He has sent Me to bind up the broken-hearted, to call to the captives liberty, and to those bound the opening of the prison; to call the year of the Lord's pleasure, and the day of vengeance" (Isaiah 61:1–2); and: "For thus says the lofty and exalted One, who dwells forever, whose name is Holy: I dwell on high and as the holy one — and with the crushed and the lowly of spirit" (Isaiah 57:15); and: "Before destruction is pride, and before stumbling is loftiness of spirit" (Proverbs 16:18).

**The seventh**: when he sees the turn-of-states of created beings in this world, the swiftness of the dissolving of kingdoms and dynasties in it, the moving of their people from state to state, the corruption of one people for the rectitude of others, and the going of all to death — as He said: "Like sheep they are appointed for Sheol; death is their shepherd" (Psalms 49:15) — he humbles himself, is not conceited concerning anything of the goods of this world, and does not lean with his heart upon anything of it, as He said: "Happy is the man who has made the Lord his trust, and has not turned to the proud" (Psalms 40:5).

When the human's thought is not free from one of these seven concepts we have mentioned, he never ceases to be humble and lowered, until humility becomes for him a binding nature that does not separate from him. When humility becomes binding upon him, it negates from him all the misfortunes of self-conceit, vainglory, and pride — as we have set forth — and he is shielded by it from error and slip, as He said: "And in order that the fear of Him be upon you, that you may not sin" (Exodus 20:20). Our early ones (peace be upon them) said: "Keep your eye on three things, and you will not come to transgression: know whence you came, and whither you are going, and before whom you are about to give judgment and reckoning. Whence you came — from a foul drop. And whither you are going — to a place of dust, worm, and maggot. And before whom you are about to give judgment and reckoning — before the King of the kings of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He" (m. Avot 3:1).
As for the conduct that the possessor of humility ought to follow — there are ten dispositions.

**The first**: knowledge of God (mighty and exalted) and of His beautiful attributes, and of how He has preferred the human over the rest of the animal — as He said: "You make him have dominion over the works of Your hands; You have set everything under his feet" (Psalms 8:7). When he discriminates the majesty of the Creator's greatness, the towering of His power, and the loftiness of His wisdom, he humbles himself before Him and abases himself in His presence — by analogy with what the Wise One has counseled: "Do not glorify yourself before a king, and do not stand in the place of the great" (Proverbs 25:6) — and how much more rightful and more emphatic is the King of kings and the Lord of lords (exalted be He from comparison and likening), as Hannah (peace be upon her) said: "There is no Holy One like the Lord, and no Rock like our God" (1 Samuel 2:2).

**The second**: knowledge of the requirements of the Law and the intellect upon him; the recitation of the Book of God; the standing upon the rational, written, and transmitted knowledge — that he may draw from these the conditions of humility and the contexts of its use.

**The third**: breadth of dispositions and patience under what he hates of speech and deed, for the sake of God (exalted be He) — as He said: "If I requited my friend with evil, or stripped my adversary empty…" (Psalms 7:5); and He said: "Do not say: 'As he did to me, so shall I do to him'" (Proverbs 24:29). Our early ones said: "Those who are insulted but do not insult, who hear themselves shamed and do not reply, who act out of love and rejoice in afflictions — concerning them Scripture says: 'And those who love Him are like the going forth of the sun in its might' (Judges 5:31)" (b. Yoma 23a). This is the one called by them *maʿavir ʿal middotav* — "one who passes over his measures."

**The fourth**: doing-the-beautiful toward people, speaking-well of them, finding excuses for them, abandoning slander and ill-speech of them, and bearing-with-tolerance their slander and ill-speech of him even when they are not deserving of that from him — as He said: "Even in your knowledge do not curse a king" (Ecclesiastes 10:20); and He said: "You loose your mouth in evil… you sit and speak against your brother, you slander your mother's son" (Psalms 50:19–20). And in the bearing-with-tolerance of slander and ill-speech: the saying of Scripture, "And Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses" — then He said: "And the man Moses was very humble" (Numbers 12:1, 3) — when he tolerated them. So too the saying of the Wise One: "Also do not give your heart to all the words that are spoken, lest you hear your servant cursing you; for many times also your heart knows that you also have cursed others" (Ecclesiastes 7:21–22).

Our early ones said: "There is a story of Rabbi Eliezer, who went down before the ark and recited twenty-four blessings of supplication and was not answered. Rabbi Akiva went down and recited 'Our Father, our King, we have none but You; our Father, our King, have mercy upon us' and was answered. A heavenly voice came forth and said: 'Not because this one is greater than that, but because this one passes over his measures and that one does not pass over his measures'" (b. Taʿanit 25b).

It has been said of one of the righteous that he passed by, on his way, the carcass of a dog, intensely foul-smelling. The disciples present with him said: "How intense is the foulness of this carcass's smell!" He said to them: "How intense is the whiteness of its teeth!" His disciples were ashamed at what had come from them of the ugly speech about it. For if speaking ill of a dog's carcass is ugly, how much more concerning a living human; and if it is fitting to find adornment upon a dog's carcass in the whiteness of its teeth, in proportion to that it is binding to find adornment upon the human who understands and reasons. He aimed only to reprove them, that ill-speech not become repeated upon their tongues and become a binding nature for them; so too, when good speech is repeated in their words, it becomes a binding nature for them — as He said: "There is no slanderer upon his tongue; he has done no evil to his neighbor" (Psalms 15:3); and He said in its opposite: "Calamities your tongue plans like a sharpened razor, working deceit; you love every devouring word, the deceitful tongue" (Psalms 52:4–6); and He said: "What can He give you and what add to you, deceitful tongue?" (Psalms 120:3); and He said: "The words of the wise man's mouth are grace, and the lips of a fool swallow him" (Ecclesiastes 10:12).

**The fifth**: humility in all the matters of his this-world — in his outer and his inner, his speech and his deed, the movements of his limbs and their stillnesses. Let his secret not contradict his public, nor his inwardness oppose his outwardness; rather let him be in his movements balanced, equal, proportionate — running on abasement and lowering before God (exalted be He) and before people, in proportion to the difference of their ranks and in proportion to what agrees with him, of them, in his religion and his this-world — as He said: "Good is the man who is gracious and lends, who orders his words with judgment" (Psalms 112:5); and our early ones said: "Be lowly of spirit before everyone" (m. Avot 4:10), and: "Be light to the head and pleasant to those of dark hour" (m. Avot 3:12).

**The sixth**: that he be lofty of aspiration and elevated of soul in the matters of the next world — never satisfied with what is present of them, never sufficed by what is possible of them. Rather let him hold his knowledge, his obedience, his power, and his exertion to be too small in his own eye, and let his aspiration be perpetually toward what is above that — as Scripture said of Jehoshaphat: "And his heart was lifted up in the ways of the Lord" (2 Chronicles 17:6). Let him reproach himself with falling-short in the matters of religion toward God and toward people; let him beseech God (mighty and exalted) for help and aid in increasing in obedience and in working at righteousness, as the Friend said: "O that my ways were directed to keep Your statutes" (Psalms 119:5).

**The seventh**: that he show forth to people his humility and the falling away of haughtiness for the very face of God; that he cast off pride, haughtiness, and self-protection in his work for God (mighty and exalted) — in private and in the assemblies of people — as Scripture said of Aaron, despite the loftiness of his rank: "And shall lift up the ashes" (Leviticus 6:3) — the Creator (exalted be He) bound him to bring out the ashes every day, perpetually, in humility before Him and the casting-off of pride. Like it is what Scripture said of David (peace be upon him): "And she saw King David leaping and dancing before the Lord, and she despised him in her heart" (2 Samuel 6:16) — and the rest of the story; and he said: "And I shall speak of Your testimonies before kings, and shall not be ashamed" (Psalms 119:46).

**The eighth**: that he be content for himself, of the means of subsistence, with what is made ready and what is possible — out of contempt for himself, slighting of himself, training himself in the bearing of his bodily appetites; and finding leisure for the discharging of the rights of God for the magnitude of His beneficence to him and the abundance of His blessing upon him — as He said: "I shall run the way of Your commandments, for You enlarge my heart" (Psalms 119:32).

**The ninth**: vindicating God against the one who has disobeyed Him. Let his tolerance toward people in his own private affair not carry him to tolerance in the matters of God (exalted be He) and the speech against His prophets, His messengers, His elect, and His chosen ones; and let him not run, in others' wronging of one another, in the way of his tolerance of their wronging him; rather let him aid the wronged, and help in the doing-of-justice from the wronger, as He said: "House of David, thus says the Lord: Render judgment in the morning, and rescue the robbed from the hand of the oppressor" (Jeremiah 21:12); and He said: "I shall break the jaws of the wrongdoer, and from his teeth I shall pluck the prey" (Job 29:17). Let him guide people to obedience to God, rebuke them, reproach them, command them in the right and forbid them the wrong with his hand, his tongue, and his heart according to his capacity; let him hasten to take up the rights of God from those who hold them; and let him not be humble nor forbearing at this — as He said of Phinehas (peace be upon him): "And Phinehas stood up and intervened, and the plague was stayed; and it was reckoned to him as righteousness for generation after generation, forever" (Psalms 106:30–31).

**The tenth**: that he be of little speech, low of voice, of little jest, of little oath-taking by God (even truthfully). Let no lie ever run upon his tongue at all; let him not enter the assemblies of frivolity; let him not rejoice in what the populace rejoices in of the world's pleasures — out of humility and lowering, not out of self-elevation and self-protection — as the Friend said: "I have not sat in the council of mockers, and I have rejoiced; from the face of Your hand I have sat alone, for You have filled me with indignation" (Jeremiah 15:17).
He said: As for the marks by which humility is verified in the humble man when they appear upon him — they are in five occurrences.

**The first**: at the time of the severity of his anger against one who has offended him by speech or deed. If he has ruled his caprice and pardoned after his capacity to take requital, in humility and lowering — that points to the soundness of his humility.

**The second**: when a misfortune in his wealth or a calamity in his household befalls him. If he prefers patience over alarm, in surrender to God's decree and contentment with His judgment — that points to the goodness of his humility and his abasement before God (mighty and exalted) — as Scripture said of Aaron (peace be upon him) at his trial in Nadab and Abihu: "And Aaron was silent" (Leviticus 10:3); and He said: "Be silent for the Lord and writhe before Him" (Psalms 37:7); and He said: "Therefore the prudent at that time shall be silent" (Amos 5:13).

**The third**: when his report spreads among people, in good or in evil. If a praiser praises him for a good deed he has done, he undermines his praiser in it; he despises it within himself; he counts it small in his eye, that God should accept it from him and be satisfied with him by it, on account of its smallness in the face of what is binding upon him of the like of that good deed. He says to his praiser: "Cut short, my brother — for it is, in the face of my sins, only as the spark of fire in the sea; and even if it had measure, how could I attain its salvation from the misfortunes of corruption that attach to it, that my Lord receive it from me, and not turn it back upon me, and not throw it in my face — as He said: 'When you come to see My face, who has sought this from your hand, to trample My courts?' (Isaiah 1:12); and: 'Bring no more vain offerings; the smoke of incense is an abomination to Me' (Isaiah 1:13)." How much more so if it was vain — it is incumbent upon him to aim at negating it from himself, and to say to the one who described him by it: "Enough, my brother, of my falling-short in what is binding upon me toward God; do not gather upon me the sin of falling-short *and* the sin of self-adornment by what I have not done; for I am more knowledgeable than you of what I bear within of sins and heedlessnesses" — as he said: "For I know my transgressions, and my sin is ever before me" (Psalms 51:5).

If he is mentioned for a bad deed he has done, he confesses against himself his falling-short in it; he aims neither at excuse nor at self-adornment in it — as Judah (peace be upon him) said: "She is more righteous than I" (Genesis 38:26). Let him not make the describer fall short, nor accuse him of lying about it. Let him not ascribe blame to him for the uncovering of it, but say to him: "My brother, what is the measure of what you have come to know of the badness of my work, in the face of what you have not known of it — concerning which God's covering of me has long endured? If the badness of my deeds and my sins were to dawn upon you, you would flee from me out of fear of God's punishment for them" — as one of the poets said: *"Were my neighbors to smell out my sins, they would flee and depart from my borders."* Job (peace be upon him) said: "If I have hidden my transgression like Adam, by concealing my iniquity in my bosom…" (Job 31:33).

If what he was ascribed of is false, let him say to the one who described him by it: "My brother, it is not from wonder, God's preserving me from the doing of what you have ascribed to me, in the face of His abundant bounty toward me. The wonder is, rather, God's covering upon me of what is more ugly and more shocking by far than what you have described me by. So cut short, my brother, and have pity on your good deeds, that they not depart from you while you do not perceive."

It has been said of one of the people of bounty: he was mentioned ill, and the report came to him; he sent to the one who slandered him a tray of the rare delicacies of his town and wrote to him: "It has reached me, my brother, that you have presented me with some of your good deeds; I saw fit to recompense you with this." One of the righteous said: "Many people may come on the Day of the Reckoning, and when their deeds are presented to them, they shall find in the registry of their good deeds good deeds they did not do, and they shall deny them; it shall be said to them: 'They were done by those who slandered you and took from your reputation.' Likewise when the good deeds of the slanderers fall, they shall seek them at that point; it shall be said to them: 'They fell from you when you slandered so-and-so and so-and-so.' So too some of them shall find in the registry of their bad deeds bad deeds they did not do, and when they deny them they shall be told: 'You caused them to fall from so-and-so and so-and-so by your slander and ill-speech of them, and you have deserved them from them, since their good deeds were insufficient against them' — as He said: 'Return to our neighbors sevenfold into their bosom the reproach with which they have reproached You, O Lord' (Psalms 79:12)." From this concept Scripture has warned us, in His saying: "Remember what the Lord your God did to Miriam by the way" (Deuteronomy 24:9).

**The fourth**: when God grants him bounty in a poured-out blessing — like surpassing knowledge, piercing understanding, abundant wealth, glory before a sultan, and what resembles these of what people customarily glory in and become conceited about — and he remains in the state of humility he was in before that, with this only adding to him devotion and abasement before God and honor and beautiful conduct toward people — as Abraham, when God praised him in His saying "Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do?" (Genesis 18:17), said: "And I am dust and ashes" (Genesis 18:27); and David (peace be upon him) said: "But I am a worm and not a man" (Psalms 22:7); and Moses and Aaron (peace be upon them) said: "And we are what?" (Exodus 16:7) — his inner being is sound and his humility is truthful. The Wise One said in this concept: "If the spirit of the ruler rises against you, do not leave your place" (Ecclesiastes 10:4).

**The fifth**: at his being reproached, and his being made to take requital for God upon himself, and the doing-of-justice to the holders of rights from his wealth. If he discharged that to its owners willingly, and hastened to take requital for God upon himself even though that was difficult upon his judgment — his humility before God, his devotion, and his lowering are made valid, as Ezra (peace be upon him) said: "We have trespassed against our God in that we have brought home foreign women" (Ezra 10:2); and: "And they gave their hand to put away their wives" (Ezra 10:19). At these occurrences and their like, the marks of humility and devotion appear from the humble; the truthfulness of their inner being toward God by them is made manifest.
He said: As for whether humility is consequent upon the excellences, or the excellences are consequent upon it —

I say in answer to this: it is known to us that the first obedience to God (mighty and exalted) on the part of the human is his disclaiming-toward-Him of the attributes of lordship, his singling-Him-out by them, and his binding-himself to all the attributes of slavehood toward God. Slavehood and lordship are of the genus of the *correlative* — the existence of which is bound to the existence of the other. The human does not deserve the name "slave" until he has a Lord, and the Lord does not deserve this name until He has a slave; for the two have the meaning of "owner" and "owned" — neither of which precedes the other in relation and naming.

So obedience to God is not made valid from the human except by his binding-upon-himself of all the attributes of slavehood toward Him: namely, humility before Him, devotion before Him, lowering toward Him, disclaiming-toward-Him of all the attributes of lordship — which are pride, glory, self-elevation, self-glorification, self-exaltation, and the like. It has been said: "Pride is the cloak of God; whoever contests God for His cloak is as one who shares it with Him." The Friend said: "The Lord reigns; He has clothed Himself with majesty; the Lord has clothed Himself, He has girded Himself with strength" (Psalms 93:1).

No excellence is made valid for the believer except after the discharging of the obligation, as He said: "Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, to attend than the fat of rams" (1 Samuel 15:22). And no obligation is made valid for him except after binding-himself to obedience to God (exalted be He). And obedience to God is not made valid from him except by singling-Him-out by all the attributes of lordship and disclaiming-toward-Him by them. And this is not made valid from him except by his binding-himself to all the attributes of slavehood toward Him. And slavehood is not made valid from him except by the truthfulness of his humility before God (exalted be He) and devotion and lowering before Him, as we have set forth.

So it is necessary from this that all the excellences and the obligations are consequent upon humility — for humility is the head and the beginning and the starting-point of them. For this reason it has become obligatory that no excellence be valid for one whose heart is empty of humility before God, and there is in his soul something of self-conceit and pride. For this reason, the head of repentance is devotion, lowering, and humility — as He said: "And My people, upon whom My name is called, shall humble themselves and pray and seek My face" (2 Chronicles 7:14); and He also said: "They have humbled themselves; I shall not destroy them" (2 Chronicles 12:7).
He said: As for whether self-conceit and humility may be gathered in the heart of the believer, or not —

We say in answer to this: self-conceit is divided into two divisions. **One of them**: the human's self-conceit in his body and in his bodily affairs and welfares. **The second division**: his self-conceit in his spiritual excellences — like knowledge, good work, and the goodness of obedience to God (mighty and exalted).

Every self-conceit that is from the side of the bodily things negates humility from the heart. It is impossible that they be gathered in a single heart, by the negation of each one of them of its companion. For when the human is conceited about anything of the matters of this world, what carries him to that is only his ignorance of the One who has bestowed the blessing upon him and his being deceived by it, and the slightness of his knowledge of the swiftness of its disappearance and its passing from him. He reckons that he is the bestower of blessing upon himself by it and the earner of it by his strength and his contrivance — as Sennacherib said: "By the strength of my hand I have done this, and by my wisdom, for I am understanding" (Isaiah 10:13); and Nebuchadnezzar said: "Is this not Babylon the great, which I have built for the house of the kingdom by the strength of my power and for the splendor of my majesty?" (Daniel 4:27); and Pharaoh said: "Mine is my Nile, and I have made myself" (Ezekiel 29:3); and you have learned what followed their saying — of the dissolving of their kingdom and the corruption of their dynasty.
As for self-conceit in spiritual excellences, it is divided into two divisions. **One of them** is blameworthy. **The second** is praiseworthy.

The blameworthy: when the man of knowledge is conceited about his knowledge and the righteous man about his work, and that carries him to seeing it as much, to declaring himself sufficient by what has come before for him of it, to contenting himself with what has been spread among people of his praise and beautiful saying. He despises people; hates them; mentions their evils; undermines the scholars of his time and the elite of his place; glorifies himself in the falling-short of his companions and in their ignorance compared to him. This is what is named by our early ones *mitkabbed bi-qlon ḥavero* — "honoring himself by the disgrace of his companion." The like of this is neither humble nor devoted.

The praiseworthy self-conceit: when the man of knowledge is conceited about his knowledge and the righteous man about his work, in thanks for the magnitude of God's blessing upon him in it and his admiring-envy of it, and that carries him to longing for the increase from it and the exertion in it; to humility before its people and being-at-home with its companions; to compassion upon their honor; to covering over their ignorance; to self-adornment toward them and love for them; to finding excuses for them and to upholding their rights — counting his excellences too small, perpetually striving in the increase from them, humbling himself for his weakness in the reaching of his hope from that, abasing himself before whomever he hopes to receive the increase by his hand, thanking God for what He has bestowed upon him of excellences, praising Him for what He has made easy for the acquisition of praiseworthy traits.

This self-conceit is not contradictory to humility, nor does it negate it. About the like of this Scripture said of Jehoshaphat (peace be upon him): "And his heart was lifted up in the ways of the Lord" (2 Chronicles 17:6) — rather, it shares with humility and adds to it, as the Wise One said: "The result of humility is the fear of the Lord" (Proverbs 22:4).
He said: As for the benefit of humility in the matters of this world and the next — there are six things. Three of them in the matters of this world; and three in the matters of the next.
As for those that are in the matters of this world —

**The first**: contentment with one's sustenance. For one upon whom self-conceit and pride have entered: this world, with what is in it, does not suffice as subsistence for him, on account of the elevation of his aspiration and his contempt for what comes to him from it. When he is humble, his soul has no measure with him; what comes to him of the world he sees as sufficiency, as subsistence and supply. There follows from this the calming of his soul and the slightness of his alarm. He eats what is present, wears what is found, sleeps where it is possible: a little of the world is enough for him along with his humility. The proud man — all of it does not close the gap of his lack, with the elevation of his soul and his towering toward it — as the Wise One said: "The righteous eats to the satisfaction of his soul, and the belly of the wicked is in want" (Proverbs 13:25).

**The second**: that the humble is patient at the descent of misfortunes upon him and the turning-against of matters, on account of his lowering and the dullness of his aspiration. The non-humble is severe in alarm and slight in patience at the descent of calamities upon him, on account of his self-conceit, the elevation of his aspiration, and the slightness of his contentment with his state — as Scripture said of one who was in this state: "How you have fallen from heaven, O Day-Star, son of dawn! How you have been cut down to the earth, low among the nations!" (Isaiah 14:12).

**The third**: that the humble is the most favored with people and the most beloved by them, and the most disposed to gather with them and to walk in their way. It has been said of one of the princes that, when he walked, he hurried in his pace; he was asked the reason for that, and he said: "Because it is more remote from vanity, and quicker for the meeting of need." One of the scholars was asked: "By what have you become a leader over the people of your time?" He said: "Because I have not met one of them but I have seen for him an excellence over me. If he was more knowledgeable than I, I said: 'This one is more obedient to God than I, on account of the surplus of his knowledge over mine.' If he was less knowledgeable than I, I said: 'This one's reckoning on the Day of the Resurrection is lighter than mine; for I disobeyed God deliberately, while he disobeys Him inadvertently.' If he was greater than I in age, I said: 'This one has more good deeds than I, on account of his preceding me in this world.' If he was less than I in age, I said: 'This one has fewer sins with God than I.' If he was equal to me in age and knowledge, I said: 'Perhaps his inner being is more sound for God than mine; for I know what has gone before me of sins, and I know nothing of what has been from him.' So I never cease honoring all of them and humbling myself before them." For this reason our early ones (peace be upon them) said: "Judge every person on the side of merit" (m. Avot 1:6); and they said: "Receive every person with a beautiful expression of face" (m. Avot 1:15); and they said: "Be lowly of spirit before everyone" (m. Avot 4:10); and they said: "A man should always be soft as a reed and not be hard as a cedar; on this account the reed merited that with it should be written the Torah-scroll, the *tefillin*, and the *mezuzot*" (b. Taʿanit 20a).
As for those that are in the matters of the next world —

**The fourth**: the humble is closer to the attainment of knowledge, by his submission to the scholars and his devotion to them and his aiming at them, as He said: "He who walks with the wise becomes wise" (Proverbs 13:20); and our early ones (of blessed memory) said: "Let your house be a meeting-place for the wise; sit in the dust of their feet, and drink in their words with thirst" (m. Avot 1:4). The aid from God upon knowledge is made valid for him by it, as He said: "He shall guide the humble in justice and shall teach the humble His way" (Psalms 25:9). The proud man — for him no true reality of knowledge is firmly fixed and he reaches no end-point of certainty of acquaintance, on account of his elevation away from aiming at the people of knowledge of God and of His Law — as He said: "The wicked, in his lofty nose, does not seek; God is not in any of his thoughts" (Psalms 10:4).

**The fifth**: that the humble hastens to the working of obediences with diligence, alertness, and eagerness; he is not haughty against any of that, nor does he despise anything of it — as our early ones said: "Be careful of a light commandment as of a heavy one, for you do not know the recompense of the commandments" (m. Avot 2:1). The one conceited with himself is slow in the working of obediences, in self-protection and self-elevation; he does not perceive himself until he falls and tumbles, as He said: "Say to the king and the queen-mother: be lowered, sit down" (Jeremiah 13:18); and He said: "Six are these that the Lord hates… haughty eyes, lying tongue…" (Proverbs 6:16–17).

**The sixth**: that the humble's work for God is accepted with God, as He said: "The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit" (Psalms 51:19); and his sin is swiftly forgiven when he repents of it, as He said: "Whoever confesses and forsakes shall obtain mercy" (Proverbs 28:13); and: "When they are humbled, you say: 'Rise up'; and the lowered of eyes He shall save" (Job 22:29).

These are ten roots from the roots of humility; from them the rest of the excellences of this lofty, elevated, exalted disposition that I have not mentioned in this gate may be made plain to you. Reflect on what I have called your attention to of them; set it before your eyes; persist in thinking about it; be eager to acquire it; tend it perpetually from your soul and your dispositions; take help in God (mighty and exalted) for it; ask Him for the gift of it from Him, and seek to be granted it from Him as a means of nearing to Him and drawing close before Him — perhaps He will make it easy for you and open for you a door and a path to it, as one of the excellent ones used to add at his prayer: "My God, guard my tongue from evil and my lips from speaking deceit" — and the rest. Beware the whisperings of your heart and caprice's deception of you in what would carry you to haughtiness, self-conceit, vanity, vainglory, the seeking of leadership, elevation, command, prohibition, and the spread of fame among people. The Wise One has said the aspect of moderation for people in this world, in his saying: "Two things I have asked of You; do not deny them to me before I die. Vanity and a word of falsehood remove far from me; poverty and wealth do not give to me; nourish me with my apportioned bread — lest I be filled and deny and say, 'Who is the Lord?' or lest I become impoverished and steal, and seize upon the name of my God" (Proverbs 30:7–9).

Wake up, O my brother! Do not be heedless of the treatment of this self-conceit from your soul and your dispositions, by the medicines I have pointed you to. Let it not prevent you from this, what you see upon the bulk of people of heedlessness in the treating of themselves of this disease — saying, "What is good enough for them is good enough for me." For the blind man, when there are present to him beneficial collyria by which his cure is possible at their use, it is not from prudence for him to delay this and say, "What is good enough for my blind companions is good enough for me." Were one of them to say to you this saying, you would consider his saying foolish, and his judgment incompetent, and would remove him from the rank of the rational. So in proportion to that, look to your soul, my brother; take it with prudence; do not be lazy in what would benefit you in your this-world and your next-world — lest you die without reaching your hopes in the excellences which are in your power to attain — as the Wise One said: "The desire of the sluggard kills him, for his hands refuse to do" (Proverbs 21:25); and he said: "I passed by the field of a sluggard and by the vineyard of a man lacking heart; and behold, it was all overgrown with thorns…  I beheld and set my heart upon it; I saw and received instruction" (Proverbs 24:30–32).
May God guide us and you to the path of His obedience, by His might and His mercy (exalted be He).
